name: Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease (IFN-gamma axis)

clinicalPearls: A group of inherited disorders in which defects along the interleukin-12/interleukin-23 to interferon-gamma circuit cripple the immune response to intracellular pathogens, leaving affected individuals uniquely vulnerable to weakly virulent mycobacteria

The hallmark is disseminated or recurrent infection with the BCG vaccine strain, non-tuberculous (environmental) mycobacteria, and non-typhoidal Salmonella, often in an otherwise healthy-looking child

Disease severity tracks the underlying genetic lesion: complete receptor defects present in infancy with overwhelming, poorly granuloma-forming disease, whereas partial defects present later with more contained, granulomatous illness
Severe reactions to BCG immunisation (BCGitis or disseminated BCGosis) in a previously well infant should trigger evaluation for this pathway

Susceptibility to intramacrophage organisms including certain fungi (histoplasma, coccidioides), and in some genotypes an added vulnerability to severe viral infection, may accompany the mycobacterial phenotype
Diagnosis rests on functional testing of the interferon-gamma axis together with molecular genetic confirmation, as several distinct genes converge on the same clinical picture

Management combines prolonged, tailored antimicrobial therapy against the offending organism with adjunctive interferon-gamma in receptor-competent forms, and consideration of haematopoietic stem cell transplantation for the most severe complete defects
reference.pathophysiology: The control of intracellular pathogens such as mycobacteria and Salmonella depends on a self-reinforcing loop between phagocytes and lymphocytes. Infected macrophages and dendritic cells release interleukin-12 and interleukin-23, which act on natural killer and T cells to drive production of interferon-gamma; that interferon-gamma in turn binds its receptor on the phagocyte, signals through the JAK-STAT1 pathway, and switches on the microbicidal machinery needed to kill the organism. Inherited defects at any node of this circuit (the interferon-gamma receptor chains, STAT1, the interleukin-12/23 subunit or its receptor, and several regulatory or transcription-factor genes) interrupt the loop, so phagocytes fail to be fully activated and organisms of low intrinsic virulence persist and spread. The depth of the defect determines whether granulomas form poorly and disease disseminates or whether infection remains comparatively localised.
additionalDifferentials: Chronic granulomatous disease and other phagocyte oxidative-burst defects
Severe combined immunodeficiency and other combined T-cell defects
GATA2 deficiency with mononuclear cytopenia and mycobacterial susceptibility
Anti-interferon-gamma autoantibody syndrome (acquired adult mycobacterial susceptibility)
Tuberculosis or leprosy in an immunocompetent host
additionalInvestigations: Functional assays of the interferon-gamma axis, including whole-blood interferon-gamma and interleukin-12 production after stimulation
Flow cytometry for interferon-gamma receptor and interleukin-12 receptor beta-1 surface expression and STAT1 phosphorylation
Targeted or panel-based genetic sequencing of the known MSMD genes
Mycobacterial and Salmonella cultures with species identification and drug-susceptibility testing
Testing for anti-interferon-gamma neutralising autoantibodies to exclude the acquired phenocopy
Assessment for HIV and other secondary immunodeficiency
Imaging to define the extent of disseminated infection and organ involvement
redFlags: Disseminated illness following BCG vaccination in an infant
Recurrent or multifocal non-tuberculous mycobacterial or non-typhoidal Salmonella infection
A family history of childhood death from disseminated mycobacterial disease
Failure of poorly formed granulomas with progressive organ infiltration in complete defects
Concurrent severe viral or intracellular fungal infection suggesting a broader signalling defect
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends heavily on genotype: partial defects and interleukin-12/23-pathway lesions often do well with prolonged antimicrobial therapy and adjunctive interferon-gamma, whereas complete interferon-gamma receptor defects carry a poor prognosis with recurrent life-threatening infection unless haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is undertaken, itself difficult in the face of active infection.
pitfalls: Attributing severe BCG or environmental mycobacterial disease to poor technique or contamination rather than an underlying host defect
Stopping antimicrobial therapy too early, as relapse is common while the immune defect persists
Giving live BCG or other live vaccines before the diagnosis is excluded in a suggestive family
Assuming a normal routine immunology screen excludes the disorder, since antibody and lymphocyte counts are typically normal
Overlooking the acquired anti-interferon-gamma autoantibody syndrome as a treatable adult mimic
references: Stiehm's Immunologic Disorders in Infants and Children
IUIS Expert Committee classification of inborn errors of immunity
management: Prolonged, species-directed combination antimycobacterial therapy guided by culture and drug-susceptibility testing, continued until immune reconstitution or lifelong in severe defects
Adjunctive recombinant interferon-gamma in interleukin-12/23-axis and partial receptor defects, recognising it is futile in complete interferon-gamma receptor deficiency or STAT1 loss-of-function
Strict avoidance of BCG and other live vaccines, with prompt treatment of any BCG-related disease
Antimicrobial and antifungal cover for accompanying non-typhoidal Salmonella and intramacrophage fungal infection
Allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation as potentially curative for complete interferon-gamma receptor deficiency
Ongoing surveillance for recurrent or disseminated infection and for toxicity of prolonged antimicrobials
Coordinated clinical immunology, infectious disease and specialist microbiology input
Genetic counselling and testing of at-risk relatives, with exclusion of the acquired anti-interferon-gamma autoantibody phenocopy
